summary:
Visitors in Moscow stand under the national framework of the Russian Federation, which has hardened sharply since 2022. The federal law signed in July 2023 bans gender transition outright: it prohibits gender-affirming surgery and removes any route to legal gender recognition on official documents. The Supreme Court's November 2023 ruling designating the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation was entered on the state's unified list of terrorist and extremist organisations on 22 March 2024, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days and deportation, and foreign governments have issued explicit warnings to LGBT travellers about this exposure.

Moscow is where the extremist designation has been applied most directly. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution, published 23 June 2025, frames LGBTQ life in Russia for the year around arrests, club raids and extremism charges, and records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024. Arrests of gay bar owners and of people displaying rainbow-flag symbols have followed the designation on extremism charges.

Moscow has no lawful assembly space for LGBT people. The city's authorities have never approved a request to hold a gay pride rally, and in 2011 the head of the Moscow Registry Office stated publicly that attempts by same-sex couples to marry in Moscow are "doomed to fail".
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement volume across the country has risen in step with severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the two preceding years.

Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or for displaying its alleged symbols as of 30 June 2025, charges brought under both the administrative and criminal codes, and called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation was reported by the Moscow Times in February 2025, in a case concerning organising that followed a court ruling in Siberia reported in January 2025.

The speed of the post-designation crackdown was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Detention carries lethal risk. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. The Moscow Times reported on 23 June 2025 that a St Petersburg queer woman described herself as "a second-class citizen" after the extremist designation.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she had found.

Advisory and asylum machinery treats the risk as country-wide. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings directed at LGBT travellers. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025, page updated 12 August 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims.
localsOnly:
Russian citizens resident in Moscow have no legal route to recognition of their gender. The July 2023 federal law removed both the surgical pathway and the administrative procedure for changing the gender marker on internal documents, passports and registry records, so residents face the ban on documentation rather than on entry.

The same law withdraws access to gender-affirming care for residents, not only visitors: the prohibition on gender reassignment surgery applies to providers inside the country, and residents have no domestic lawful provider to turn to.

For residents, the extremist designation applies without the deportation backstop available to foreign nationals. Displaying a rainbow symbol, sharing flagged material, or associating with an entity listed under the designation can attract administrative or criminal extremism charges; the 101 convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch through 30 June 2025 were entered against people inside the country.

There is no lawful assembly or registration route in Moscow. Pride applications have never been approved by the city authorities, and same-sex couples seeking to marry in Moscow are refused at the registry office, a position stated on the record by the head of the Moscow Registry Office in 2011.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the case against the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, arrested in Moscow in late December 2024, is not stated in the sources assembled here; only the arrest is sourced.

The February 2025 report of Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-extremism designation identifies the case as concerning organising and places the underlying court ruling in Siberia in January 2025, but the sentence length, the court and the defendant's identity are not sourced in this inventory.

Whether Moscow operates a standing legal prohibition on pride events, or refuses each application individually, is unresolved; the sourced fact is that no request has ever been approved.

The Moscow Registry Office statement about same-sex marriage attempts dates from 2011. Whether it still describes current registry practice in Moscow, as opposed to the position under the 2024 constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman, is not sourced here.

Several national-level facts in this record rest on a Wikipedia country overview rather than primary legal texts: the November 2023 designation, the 22 March 2024 list entry, and the July 2023 ban on gender transition. The statute text and the Supreme Court judgment are not quoted directly in the inventory.
